title: Peter and Cornelius (Acts 10)
hook: a vision of a sheet of animals teaches Peter that God shows no partiality
carry: no one is unclean to god

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Damascus road: Saul was knocked down, and Ananias called him brother. Your line was the scales fall. Did you change your mind about anything, out loud? Day seventy-seven.

Two men, thirty miles apart, who would never normally share a meal. In the port city of Caesarea lives Cornelius, a Roman army officer, a centurion. He's not Jewish, but he prays to the God of Israel, gives generously to the poor, and his whole household honors God. One afternoon an angel tells him: send to the town of Joppa for a man named Peter. Meanwhile, in Joppa, around noon the next day, Peter goes up on a flat rooftop to pray. He's hungry. Lunch is being made downstairs. And he falls into a kind of trance. Today: what Peter saw on the roof.
screen: `A ROMAN CENTURION WHO PRAYS.` → `SEND FOR PETER.` → `A HUNGRY MAN ON A ROOF.`

segments.voice: He sees the sky open and something like a great sheet let down by its four corners, full of every kind of animal, including ones the Law of Moses says not to eat. And a voice, in the Douay-Rheims: "Arise, Peter; kill, and eat." Peter is a faithful Jew. He refuses: he has never eaten anything unclean. And the voice answers: "That which God hath cleansed, do not thou call common." This happens three times. Then the sheet is taken up, and Peter sits there puzzled. At that exact moment, Cornelius's messengers knock at the gate. Peter goes with them to Caesarea and walks into a Gentile's home, something he'd never have done before, and he tells them what the vision meant. It wasn't really about food. "God hath shewed to me, to call no man common or unclean." Then: "In very deed I perceive, that God is not a respecter of persons." That old phrase translates a Greek word that literally means a face-taker, someone who judges by the face in front of them. God doesn't. And while Peter is still talking, the Holy Spirit falls on Cornelius and his whole household, just as at Pentecost, and they're baptized. Catholics call this the moment the door opened to every nation, and the word catholic itself means universal. Many Jews today keep the food laws faithfully, and this story isn't a verdict on them. Its point, in Peter's own words, is people. So that was the week: the charcoal fire, the Ascension, Pentecost, koinonia, Stephen, Ananias on the Damascus road, and Peter and Cornelius, the face-taker. The fire spreads.
screen: `A SHEET FULL OF ANIMALS.` · `WHAT GOD HATH CLEANSED.` · `NOT FOOD: PEOPLE.` · `NO FACE-TAKER.` · then, large: `GOD IS NOT A RESPECTER OF PERSONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome someone different from you. Settle and breathe. Think of a kind of person you'd rarely sit down to eat with: a different background, politics, age, faith. Picture one real person, if you can. Picture them at your table, and you listening. Notice any quiet voice that says not them. Just notice it. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name. If you don't, just hold their face in your mind kindly. The bell holds the time.
face-taker. What God is not, Peter realized, after a sheet full of animals and a door opened to every nation.
Your line: no one is unclean to god. Today, sit with someone you'd usually walk past, even for five minutes. Day seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics read the story of Peter and Cornelius in the Easter season as the opening of the Church to every nation, the root of the word catholic, universal.

fork.setup: you're Peter. a voice from heaven tells you to eat animals you've never eaten in your life. what do you say?
options: refuse: you've never eaten anything unclean.
fork.reveal: he refuses, three times. and the voice says: "that which God hath cleansed, do not thou call common."

original.note: Greek: a face-taker, someone who judges by appearance. God, Peter says, is not one.

trapdoor: what you thought: a vision that said Christians can eat anything.
what it means: Peter learns that God shows no partiality, and the Church opens its door to every nation.
what a scholar hears: prosopolemptes, a face-taker, a word found only here in the New Testament. and catholic comes from the Greek for universal, throughout the whole.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Acts 10:13, 15, 28 and 34 given from memory; confirm.
Joppa to Caesarea is roughly 30–35 miles; script says 'thirty miles'.
προσωπολήμπτης occurs only in Acts 10:34 in the New Testament (the Bible, as the trapdoor says, if counting the Septuagint too); confirm or change to 'in the New Testament'.

Respect for Jewish dietary law: the script says the story isn't a verdict on Jews who keep the food laws and quotes Peter's own application to people. Keeper and interfaith reviewer should confirm the framing.
